title: Timing of rate hikes only doubt after hot GDP data
full_text:
Michele Bullock’s Reserve Bank board faces an ugly policy dilemma. The effects of its previous interest rate hikes are still working through the economy, but inflation remains high and economic growth is holding up better than expected.
While hikes may push the economy into recession, the RBA may have little choice after higher than expected inflation, household spending and growth numbers in the last week.
Whether at the September or November meeting, the consensus among economists is shifting towards a restart of rate hikes as the latest data are stronger than forecast despite three increases in the cash rate this year to 4.35 per cent.
After Wednesday’s data showed annual GDP rose 2.1 per cent for the June quarter, versus 1.9 per cent expected by the RBA, market pricing on the chance of a September 29 rate hike hit 68 per cent.
The market was more than fully priced for a 25 basis points rate hike by November. It was also 80 per cent of the way towards pricing in two rate hikes by February.
Some board members may continue to argue that rates are already high enough, but some of the upside risks flagged last month – a prolonged Middle East conflict, cost pressures being passed through more fully than assumed, and stronger than forecast demand – now look to be playing out.
Global X ETFs’ Marc Jocum warns the quality of growth is questionable, with Australia leaning on “two growth hacks – more people and more government spending” – rather than genuine productivity gains. But the data “make it increasingly difficult for the RBA to justify sitting on its hands”.
Households proved more resilient than expected, helped by a surprise 0.6 per cent rise in real disposable income. Much of the extra spending went on electric vehicles, as higher petrol prices and the Middle East conflict prompted many to switch away from petrol cars and cancel overseas trips.
CBA notes fewer Australians travelling overseas meant “more household spending occurred in Australia, adding to domestic capacity constraints and inflationary pressures”.
For the RBA, the data leaves little room to sit still. Growth is running close to – or perhaps above – the economy’s speed limit, inflation risks are crystallising, and the labour market has yet to show enough slack. Barring a sharp deterioration in upcoming jobs data, the odds increasingly favour another rate rise, either in September or in November.
